readerTitle: Sales tripled. Why changing course may still be right
caseNote: 가상 사례 (중소 건설사 대상 기장 대행 서비스, 친환경 포장 상자 제조사) · 모든 수치는 설명용. 개념 출처는 Eric Ries, The Lean Startup
insight: 계속할지 방향을 틀지는 매출 총액이 아니라, 시도할 때마다 핵심 비율이 움직이는지로 판단한다.
misconception: 매출이 늘고 있으면 계속 가면 되고, 매출이 정체되면 방향을 바꿔야 한다. 피벗은 처음부터 다시 시작하는 것이다.

sources.text: Ries, E. (2011). The Lean Startup. Crown Business. (pivot or persevere, pivot의 정의와 유형)

factChecks.note: Ries의 피벗 정의는 원문 인용이 아니라 '제품·전략·성장 방식에 대한 새로운 핵심 가설을 시험하기 위한 구조화된 방향 수정'이라는 취지로 풀어 썼습니다. 게시 전 원문 표현을 확인하세요.

기장 대행 사례 수치(월 매출 $4,000→$14,000, 영업 통화 월 40→140건, 계약률 10% 유지, 3개월 유지율 30% 유지)는 설명용입니다. 매출은 고객 누적과 이탈을 정밀하게 모델링한 값이 아니며, '노력이 늘어서 매출이 늘었다'는 방향만 보여줍니다. 통화 수 3.5배, 매출 3.5배로 맞췄습니다(140÷40=3.5, 14,000÷4,000=3.5).
차트의 두 회사 계약률(A: 10% 고정, B: 4→6→8→10→12%)과 포장 제조사 재주문율(15→22→31→38%)은 설명용 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: Sales tripled. Why changing course may still be right
body: A small bookkeeping service for builders grew monthly revenue from $4,000 to $14,000 in six months.
The founder is thinking about changing who the business serves. That sounds reckless. The numbers underneath say it might be the smart move.

image.label: A rising revenue line next to a flat line
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 사무실 책상 위 화이트보드에 가파르게 올라가는 초록 선과, 그 아래 완전히 평평한 회색 선. 창업자가 평평한 선을 손가락으로 가리키는 모습. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Keep going, or change course?
body: You run that bookkeeping service. Revenue has more than tripled. But you also hired a second salesperson and tripled your sales calls.
You tried five changes to the offer. Through all of them, 1 in 10 calls became a client, and only 3 in 10 clients stayed past three months.

options.text: Keep going. Revenue is growing fast
options.feedback: You keep momentum, but the growth comes from more effort, not a better offer. Costs will keep rising with it.

options.text: Change one core part, like who you serve, and keep what you've learned
options.feedback: You give up a familiar plan to test a new one, while keeping your skills, tools and lessons. That's the idea in this lesson.

options.text: Shut it down and start a new business
options.feedback: You stop wasting effort, but you throw away six months of learning that a smaller change could reuse.

cards.title: Growth came from effort, not from the offer.
body: Revenue and calls both grew 3.5 times. The **rates** did not move at all. Five changes, zero effect.

cards.title: Pivot or persevere
body: **Persevere** means keeping your core plan and improving it. **Pivot** means changing one core assumption, such as the customer, the problem or how you charge, while keeping what you learned.

Eric Ries made the question central in *The Lean Startup*. The test is simple: when you make a change, does the rate that matters move? If it keeps rising, persevere. If changes stop moving it, pivot.
cards.softwareNote: In software, the rate is often the share of new users still active after a few weeks. If release after release leaves that number flat, more ad spend won't fix it.

cards.title: The slower business is the one to back.
body: Firm B earns less today. But every change it makes lifts its close rate. Firm A's changes do nothing.

groups.label: Firm A: calls that become clients
Firm B: calls that become clients

cards.callout: Judge the direction of the rate, not the size of the total.

cards.title: A pivot keeps most of the business.
body: A good pivot changes one big thing and reuses the rest:
list: **New customer:** same service, sold to restaurants instead of builders
**New problem:** same clients, but solve cash flow instead of bookkeeping
**New way to charge:** a fixed monthly fee instead of hourly
**Zoom in:** turn the one feature people love into the whole offer
cards.callout: Starting over is not a pivot. It throws away what you learned.

cards.title: Decide the test before you see the results.
body: Early numbers are noisy. Ten sales calls can't tell you much, so pivoting after a bad week is just guessing.
Pivoting too often is also a trap. A new direction every month means no idea gets a fair test.
Before each change, write down the rate you expect to move, by how much, and the date you'll decide.

cards.title: Now it's a box factory.
body: You make eco-friendly shipping boxes for small online shops. Revenue has been flat for four months because you paused marketing.
Meanwhile you lowered prices, sped up delivery and added sizes. Repeat orders rose from 15% to 22%, 31%, then 38%. An adviser says flat revenue means it's time to pivot to wholesale.

options.text: Persevere, and start spending on growth again
options.feedback: Each change moved the rate that matters, so the offer is improving. Revenue was flat because effort was flat.

options.text: Pivot to wholesale, since revenue isn't growing
options.feedback: You'd chase a bigger market but abandon an offer that is clearly getting stronger with each change.

options.text: Keep tweaking the offer with no end date
options.feedback: Improving is good, but without a target and a deadline you can't tell when it's time to grow or to stop.

cards.title: Persevere while changes move the rate. Pivot when they stop.
body: Totals tell you how hard you're pushing. Rates tell you whether the plan is working.
**Try it today:** pick the one rate that matters most to your business. List your last three changes and whether each one moved it.
